plan.title: Confident English for Real Life
plan.description: A focused four-week path for an Arabic-speaking B1 learner who wants clearer speech and more confidence in travel, daily life, and work conversations.

weeks.title: Travel with confidence
weeks.description: Handle airport plans and common travel questions clearly.

units.title: At the airport
units.description: Build a complete language toolkit for planning and navigating a flight.

lessons.title: Airport essentials
lessons.description: Learn high-value words used before and during a flight.
objectives: Use each term in a realistic sentence
lessons.personalization_reason: Travel is one of your selected goals, so the plan begins with language you can use immediately.

content.intro: Focus on meaning and natural combinations, not isolated translation.

activities.definition: A detailed plan for a journey, including places and times.
examples: I emailed the itinerary to everyone in our group.
Our itinerary includes a two-hour stop in Istanbul.

activities.definition: A period of waiting between two parts of a flight.
examples: We have a short layover in Doha.
Is the layover long enough to leave the airport?

activities.definition: A small bag that a passenger takes onto an aircraft.
examples: My laptop is in my carry-on.
This ticket includes one carry-on.

activities.prompt: Which word means a planned route and schedule for a journey?
activities.explanation: An itinerary records the route, times, and activities planned for a journey.

activities.prompt: We have a three-hour _____ in Dubai before the next flight.
activities.explanation: A layover or stopover is time spent waiting between connecting flights.

lessons.title: Talking about travel plans
lessons.description: Choose natural future forms for intentions and arrangements.
objectives: Use the present continuous for fixed arrangements
lessons.personalization_reason: This grammar turns the travel vocabulary you just learned into useful plans and answers.

content.intro: English uses different future forms depending on whether a plan is an intention or a fixed arrangement.

activities.title: Intentions: be going to
activities.explanation: Use be going to when you have decided what you intend to do, but the details may not be formally arranged.
key_points: Use am, is, or are before going to.
The main verb stays in its base form.
examples: I am going to visit my cousin.
We are going to book a hotel tonight.

activities.title: Arrangements: present continuous
activities.explanation: Use the present continuous when the arrangement is fixed, often with a specific time or place.
key_points: Use am, is, or are plus the -ing form.
Include a future time expression when context is unclear.
examples: We are flying on Friday morning.
I am meeting the driver at six.

activities.prompt: The tickets are booked. We _____ to Cairo at 8:00 tomorrow.
activities.explanation: The booked flight is a fixed arrangement, so the present continuous is natural.

activities.prompt: I have decided to travel in August. I _____ visit Turkey.
activities.explanation: Going to expresses the intention you have already decided on.

lessons.title: Clear TH sounds
lessons.description: Contrast /θ/ and /ð/ without replacing them with /s/, /z/, /t/, or /d/.
lessons.personalization_reason: These sounds do not exist as the same phonemes in many Arabic varieties and often benefit from focused placement practice.

content.intro: Use the instructions here to understand the movement, then use the Practice tab when you want acoustic scoring.

activities.title: Voiceless TH
activities.instructions: Place the tip of your tongue lightly between your teeth and let air continue through the gap without voicing.
tips: Do not stop the air as you would for /t/.
Keep the tongue relaxed and visible in a mirror.

activities.title: Voiced TH
activities.instructions: Keep the same tongue position, but add vibration in your throat while the air continues.
tips: Touch your throat to check for vibration.
Avoid closing the tongue contact into /d/.

activities.prompt: Which word begins with the voiced sound /ð/?
activities.explanation: Those begins with voiced /ð/; think and three begin with voiceless /θ/.

lessons.title: Airport checkpoint
lessons.description: Check your vocabulary, grammar, and sound awareness.
objectives: Confirm readiness to move to the next context
lessons.personalization_reason: A short checkpoint prevents the plan from advancing based only on lesson completion.

content.intro: Score at least 70% to consider this unit secure. Mock progress still allows review without permanently saving results.

activities.prompt: Which item normally stays with you inside the aircraft cabin?
activities.explanation: A carry-on is the bag you take into the cabin.

activities.prompt: The reservation is confirmed. We _____ at the hotel on Monday.
activities.explanation: A confirmed reservation is a fixed arrangement, so present continuous is appropriate.

activities.prompt: Which pair contains one /θ/ word and one /ð/ word?
activities.explanation: Think starts with /θ/, while those starts with /ð/.

weeks.title: Everyday conversations
weeks.description: Make requests, arrange appointments, and distinguish /p/ from /b/.

units.title: Appointments and errands
units.description: Handle common service conversations efficiently and politely.
objectives: Avoid confusing words such as park and bark

lessons.title: Appointment language
lessons.description: Learn verbs and nouns for scheduling everyday services.
objectives: Schedule, confirm, and reschedule an appointment
lessons.personalization_reason: Service conversations are frequent, short, and ideal for building speaking confidence.

content.intro: Learn the complete phrase around each word so it is easier to retrieve during a real conversation.

activities.definition: To arrange a new time for an event or appointment.
examples: Could I reschedule my appointment for Thursday?

activities.definition: The times when someone or something is free to be used.
examples: What availability do you have this week?

activities.definition: To state that an arrangement is definite or correct.
examples: I am calling to confirm tomorrow's appointment.

activities.prompt: You cannot attend at the original time. What do you need to do?
activities.explanation: Reschedule means arranging a different time.

lessons.title: Polite requests
lessons.description: Adjust direct questions so they sound cooperative and natural.
objectives: Use could and would in service conversations
lessons.personalization_reason: Polite request frames reduce hesitation because you can reuse them in many settings.

content.intro: A small change in structure can make a request sound much more natural.

activities.title: Could you ...?
activities.explanation: Use could you plus a base verb to ask another person to do something.
key_points: Keep the main verb in its base form.
Use please when it adds warmth, not in every sentence.
examples: Could you check the time for me?
Could you repeat that, please?

activities.title: Would it be possible ...?
activities.explanation: Use this longer frame for a careful request, especially when the request may inconvenience someone.
key_points: Follow it with to plus a base verb.
The phrase is polite but should remain concise.
examples: Would it be possible to move the appointment?
Would it be possible to call me later?

activities.prompt: Which request is grammatically correct and polite?
activities.explanation: Could you is followed by the base form repeat, without to.

lessons.title: The /p/ and /b/ contrast
lessons.description: Use airflow and voicing to keep similar words distinct.
objectives: Release /p/ with a puff of air
lessons.personalization_reason: The /p/–/b/ contrast is a useful Arabic-L1 priority because substitutions can change word meaning.

content.intro: Hold a small piece of paper in front of your mouth: /p/ should move it more strongly than /b/.

activities.title: Airflow for /p/
activities.instructions: Close both lips, build air pressure, then release it without voicing.
tips: Check for a small puff of air.
Do not add a vowel before the consonant.

activities.title: Voicing for /b/
activities.instructions: Close both lips and release them while your vocal folds vibrate.
tips: Touch your throat to feel voicing.

activities.prompt: Which sound is normally released with a stronger puff of air at the start of an English word?
activities.explanation: Initial English /p/ is normally aspirated, while /b/ is voiced and less strongly aspirated.

lessons.title: Everyday conversation checkpoint
objectives: Use this week's language accurately in short situations
lessons.personalization_reason: This checkpoint combines form and meaning instead of testing isolated definitions only.

content.intro: Choose the response that would work in a real service conversation.

activities.prompt: You need a different appointment time. Which sentence is best?
activities.explanation: The sentence combines the correct verb with a polite request frame.

activities.prompt: Would it be possible _____ move the meeting to Tuesday?
activities.explanation: Would it be possible is followed by to plus the base verb.

weeks.title: English at work
weeks.description: Report progress, clarify problems, and contrast /f/ with /v/.
objectives: Connect past actions to the present

units.title: Projects and problem solving
units.description: Communicate progress and ask for clarification in a professional setting.

lessons.title: Project vocabulary
lessons.description: Learn reusable words for discussing tasks and problems.
lessons.personalization_reason: Workplace English supports your goal of speaking more confidently in practical conversations.

content.intro: These words are useful in both technical and non-technical projects.

activities.definition: The latest time by which a task must be completed.
examples: We can still meet the Friday deadline.

activities.definition: A task or goal that is more important than others.
examples: Fixing the login issue is our first priority.

activities.definition: To identify and solve the cause of a problem.
examples: We are troubleshooting the connection problem.

activities.prompt: Which verb means finding and fixing the cause of a technical problem?
activities.explanation: To troubleshoot is to investigate and solve a problem.

lessons.title: Reporting recent progress
lessons.description: Use the present perfect when a past action matters now.
objectives: Choose it for current results and unfinished time
lessons.personalization_reason: Project updates often focus on what has been completed and what remains.

content.intro: Use have or has plus the past participle when the result is connected to now.

activities.title: Current result
activities.explanation: The present perfect highlights a completed action whose result is important now.
key_points: Use have with I, you, we, and they.
Use has with he, she, and it.
examples: We have fixed the login issue.
She has completed the report.

activities.title: Unfinished time
activities.explanation: Use the present perfect for actions during a time period that has not finished.
key_points: Common frames include today, this week, and so far.
examples: I have answered six emails today.
We have finished two tasks this week.

activities.prompt: The team _____ fixed the connection problem.
activities.explanation: Team is treated as singular here, so use has plus fixed.

lessons.title: The /f/ and /v/ contrast
lessons.description: Keep continuous air for both sounds and add voicing for /v/.
lessons.personalization_reason: This contrast is worth explicit practice because /v/ is absent from some Arabic sound systems.

content.intro: For both sounds, touch the lower lip lightly to the upper teeth and let air continue.

activities.title: Voiceless /f/
activities.instructions: Keep the airflow continuous without vibration in your throat.
tips: Hold the sound briefly to check the airflow.

activities.title: Voiced /v/
activities.instructions: Use the same lip and teeth position while adding steady vibration.
tips: Touch your throat to verify voicing.

activities.prompt: What is the main articulatory difference between /f/ and /v/?
activities.explanation: The mouth position is similar, but /v/ adds vocal-fold vibration.

lessons.title: Work update checkpoint
lessons.description: Check your ability to give a short, accurate project update.
objectives: Combine project vocabulary with recent-result grammar
lessons.personalization_reason: The checkpoint rehearses the concise updates used in real meetings.

content.intro: Read each situation as if you were giving an update to a colleague.

activities.prompt: Which update emphasizes a useful result now?

options.text: We have fixed the main issue.
We has fix the main issue.

activities.explanation: Have fixed is the correct present-perfect form for we.

activities.prompt: Finishing the urgent task is our top _____.
activities.explanation: A top priority is the task judged most important.

weeks.title: Speak in connected ideas
weeks.description: Organize longer answers and make important words easier to hear.
objectives: Apply word stress and manageable thought groups

units.title: Clear longer answers
units.description: Move from correct sentences to organized, listener-friendly speech.

lessons.title: Signposting expressions
lessons.description: Guide the listener through an explanation or opinion.
objectives: Introduce, add, and conclude an idea clearly
lessons.personalization_reason: Reusable signposts make longer answers easier to produce and easier to follow.

content.intro: Use signposts selectively; one clear phrase is better than several fillers.

activities.definition: A phrase used to introduce your opinion.
examples: In my view, remote work is useful for focused tasks.

activities.definition: A phrase used to introduce evidence or an illustration.
examples: Some tools save time. For example, templates reduce repeated work.

activities.definition: Considering everything; used to introduce a general conclusion.
examples: Overall, the project was successful despite the delay.

activities.prompt: Which expression naturally introduces a concluding judgment?
activities.explanation: Overall introduces a conclusion based on all the information discussed.

lessons.title: Linking contrast and reason
lessons.description: Connect ideas without producing overly long sentences.
objectives: Use because to give a reason
lessons.personalization_reason: Clear connectors help turn short answers into organized B1–B2 responses.

content.intro: Choose one connector that matches the relationship between the ideas.

activities.title: Contrast with although
activities.explanation: Although introduces an idea that contrasts with the main result.
key_points: Although is followed by a complete clause.
Do not add but to the same two-clause pattern.
examples: Although the task was difficult, we finished it on time.

activities.title: Reason with because
activities.explanation: Because introduces the reason for a situation or opinion.
key_points: Because is followed by a subject and verb.
Keep the reason close to the claim it supports.
examples: I prefer the morning flight because it arrives before noon.

activities.prompt: _____ the call was short, we solved the problem.
activities.explanation: Although marks the contrast between the short call and the successful result.

lessons.title: Stress and thought groups
lessons.description: Make key words prominent and divide longer sentences into manageable groups.
objectives: Pause at meaning boundaries rather than after every word
lessons.personalization_reason: Sentence-level clarity depends on rhythm and grouping as well as individual consonants.

content.intro: Capital letters below indicate the important word, not shouting. A slash marks a natural thought-group boundary.

activities.title: Prominent content words
activities.instructions: Make the important noun, verb, adjective, or adverb slightly longer and clearer than surrounding function words.
tips: Do not stress every word equally.
Choose the word that carries the new information.

activities.title: Meaningful groups
activities.instructions: Group words that belong together, then use a brief boundary before the next idea.
tips: Avoid pausing between an article and its noun.
Use the boundary to prepare the next idea, not to take a dramatic breath.

practice_items.text: Although the task was difficult / we finished on time.
In my view / the morning flight is better.

activities.prompt: What usually happens to the word carrying new information?

options.text: It must be followed by a long pause

activities.explanation: New or contrastive information commonly receives greater prominence.

lessons.title: Real-life communication checkpoint
lessons.description: Review the language choices that support a clear extended answer.
objectives: Organize and support a practical opinion
lessons.personalization_reason: The final checkpoint combines skills across the plan instead of measuring one isolated rule.

content.intro: This mock checkpoint tests language awareness. A future speaking task can add live delivery evidence when an expected prompt is defined.

activities.prompt: Which response is best organized?

options.text: In my view, the morning flight is better because it arrives early.
Morning flight better arrive early because.

activities.explanation: The response introduces an opinion and supports it with a clear reason.

activities.prompt: _____ the deadline was tight, the team completed the project.
activities.explanation: Although introduces the contrast between the difficult condition and successful result.

activities.prompt: Which phrase should introduce a general conclusion?
activities.explanation: Overall signals that you are giving a conclusion based on the whole discussion.
